label: Lightning Rod Records
description: Isbell's third solo album, his second billed to the 400 Unit, splits the difference between the Southern-rock muscle of his Truckers years and the quieter, more personal writing to come. 'Alabama Pines' is a homesick ballad about drifting away from a small town, while 'Codeine' works as a slow-building blues about addiction that points straight at the sobriety songs on 'Southeastern'. It still sounds like a full-band record made by a road-hardened Southern rock outfit rather than the stripped-back singer-songwriter Isbell would soon become.
lineage: Continues the Southern storytelling-rock lane of Isbell's Drive-By Truckers years and his self-titled 400 Unit debut, while its darker, sobriety-tinged songs point directly ahead to Southeastern and the more confessional solo run that followed.
borderline_note: Transitional record between Isbell's V3 Southern-rock era and his V7 solo-Americana run; placed V3 primary/V7 secondary by sound, per assignment.

label: Southeastern Records
description: Recorded soon after Isbell got sober, this is a quieter, more exposed record than anything he made with Drive-By Truckers, built around close-mic'd acoustic guitar and plainspoken lyrics. 'Elephant' tells a friend's cancer death without flinching, while 'Cover Me Up' turns getting clean and falling in love into the same vow. It works as a solo-singer-songwriter record for people who want Isbell's storytelling stripped of full-band noise.
lineage: Grows out of the character-driven songwriting Isbell developed on Decoration Day and The Dirty South with Drive-By Truckers, but strips it down into a solo Americana mode that set the template for his own new-outlaw/neo-traditional-adjacent solo run and influenced a generation of confessional Nashville songwriters.

label: Southeastern
description: A calmer, more settled follow-up to Southeastern, written from a place of sobriety and a new marriage rather than crisis. 'Speed Trap Town' follows a young man leaving a dying small town after his father's death, and '24 Frames' turns quick, plainspoken lines into a warning about how fast a good life can unravel. The full band returns but stays restrained, favoring pedal steel and warm mid-tempo arrangements over the loud guitars of his Truckers days.
lineage: Follows directly from Southeastern's confessional Americana, keeping the same small-town character studies that trace back to his Drive-By Truckers writing while moving further from Southern rock toward a settled, roots-country sound.

label: Southeastern
description: The full 400 Unit returns in force here, with louder guitars than Isbell's two prior solo records and a more overtly political streak. 'White Man's World' is a blunt reckoning with inherited privilege, and 'If We Were Vampires' turns a plain conversation about mortality into a wedding-ready ballad about loving someone you will one day lose. It sits between his hushed solo records and his old Southern-rock band records, with the storytelling of both.
lineage: Reunites Isbell with a full rock band after two mostly-acoustic solo albums, pulling the sound back toward the harmonized-guitar Southern rock of his Drive-By Truckers years while keeping Southeastern's confessional lyric focus.

label: Southeastern
description: A career-spanning live set recorded at Nashville's Ryman Auditorium, drawing mostly from the Southeastern-through-Nashville Sound run with the full 400 Unit behind him. 'Hope the High Road' and '24 Frames' get fuller, more muscular arrangements than their studio versions, while 'Cover Me Up' becomes a communal singalong with the room clearly audible. It is a document of Isbell as an arena-ready bandleader rather than the hushed solo performer of his records.
lineage: Pulls its setlist from the solo Americana catalog that began with Southeastern, showing how those songs grew into full-band showpieces once the 400 Unit had toured them for years.

label: Southeastern
description: A record about talking to people who are gone, whether through death, addiction or old versions of yourself, dressed in fuller, more atmospheric arrangements than his previous two 400 Unit albums. 'Dreamsicle' remembers a childhood shaped by a parent's drinking, and 'River' closes the album on a slow, string-touched meditation on mortality. It is denser and more layered in the mix than Southeastern, but keeps the same plainspoken, first-person songwriting.
lineage: Continues the confessional Americana songwriting Isbell established on Southeastern, adding more elaborate studio arrangements while keeping the small-cast, first-person storytelling that traces back to his Drive-By Truckers work.

label: Southeastern
description: A one-off charity covers album made after Georgia voted for Joe Biden in 2020, with Isbell and the 400 Unit reworking songs written by Georgia artists across soul, Southern rock and jangle-pop. R.E.M.'s 'Nightswimming' and Otis Redding's 'I've Been Loving You Too Long' sit alongside the Allman Brothers Band's 'In Memory of Elizabeth Reed', with a rotating cast of guest singers taking turns at the mic. It is a genre-hopping detour rather than a proper Isbell studio record, closer to a mixtape than a statement.
lineage: A covers side project rather than a step in Isbell's own songwriting arc, but it ties his Southeastern-era band directly back to the Georgia soul and Southern-rock records (R.E.M., the Allman Brothers Band, Otis Redding) that fed the wider V3/V7 lineage.
borderline_note: Included per assignment as a verified Collab/covers Deep cut; not part of Isbell's core songwriting catalog.

label: Southeastern Records
description: A leaner, more direct 400 Unit record after the denser production of Reunions, with the band cut loose to stretch out on longer arrangements. 'Cast Iron Skillet' strings together small-town parables about judgment and consequence, and the closing 'Miles' runs past seven minutes as a slow-building meditation on aging. It is the sound of the full band playing to its own strengths rather than chasing a single studio mood.
lineage: Returns to the full-band, harmonized-guitar approach of The Nashville Sound after the more orchestrated Reunions, keeping Isbell's storytelling lineage running from Drive-By Truckers through his own solo catalog.

label: Southeastern
description: Isbell's first fully solo acoustic record since Sirens of the Ditch, cut fast with no 400 Unit and just his own voice and guitar filling the space. 'Bury Me' and the title track work through the end of his marriage in blunt, unsparing detail, while 'Good While It Lasted' takes a plainer, more forgiving view of the same breakup. It strips away nearly two decades of full-band arrangements to leave just the bare songwriting.
lineage: A return to the unaccompanied, acoustic-singer-songwriter mode of Isbell's pre-400 Unit debut Sirens of the Ditch, after seven straight albums made with the full band.
